title: Choosing the right ownership primitive in hot code
question: How do you choose between raw pointers, std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr, and std::weak_ptr in performance-sensitive C++ systems?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the code on a latency-critical path or mostly control-plane code?
answerOutline: Tie the answer to hot-path tradeoffs
sampleAnswer: I start by modeling ownership explicitly: `std::unique_ptr<T>` is my default when one object owns another because it has the same indirection cost as a raw pointer but encodes lifetime in the type system. `std::shared_ptr<T>` is for true shared lifetime, not convenience; `auto p = std::make_shared<Book>();` is fine for control-plane graphs, but every copy can imply ref-count traffic and a larger control footprint that I would avoid in a hot market-data path. Raw pointers and references are still useful as non-owning observers, for example `void process(const Book* book)` or `Book& book`, as long as the owning lifetime is obvious and stable. If a back-reference is needed, I prefer `std::weak_ptr<T>` to break cycles, or better yet redesign ownership around IDs, arenas, or parent-owned storage so the cycle never exists. In senior systems work, the strong answer is not memorizing pointer types; it is connecting ownership semantics to cache behavior, atomic overhead, and failure modes such as leaks or use-after-free.
commonMistakes: Using shared_ptr as a default because it feels safe
Confusing observing pointers with owning pointers
followUps: When is `make_shared` worse than separate allocations?
Would you allow shared_ptr on a latency-critical order path?
seniorExtension: Discuss how intrusive reference counting or epoch-based reclamation changes the trade space compared with standard smart pointers.

title: Avoiding dangling references with views and spans
question: What lifetime mistakes commonly happen with std::string_view, std::span, and references, and how do you avoid them?

title: Placement new and custom storage safely
question: When would you use placement new or a memory pool in C++, and what correctness risks come with it?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the pool for fixed-size hot objects or a general-purpose allocator replacement?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating lifetime correctness under manual allocation
answerOutline: State why custom storage is used
Explain object lifetime start and end
sampleAnswer: I use placement new or fixed-size pools when I need deterministic allocation behavior, fewer calls into the general allocator, or better locality for many short-lived objects such as orders or decoded messages. For example, `void* slot = pool.allocate(); Order* o = new (slot) Order(args...);` starts object lifetime in preallocated storage, but I then own destruction explicitly with `o->~Order(); pool.deallocate(slot);`. The main risks are violating alignment, reusing storage before the old object's lifetime has ended, forgetting destruction for non-trivial types, and accidentally treating raw bytes as if an object still exists there. I also care about debugging cost: pools can hide leaks and double-destroys, so I often add generation counters, poison patterns, or debug-mode fallback to the system allocator. A strong senior answer acknowledges that pools can improve latency, but only if the lifetime protocol is simpler than the bugs they invite.

Ignoring alignment requirements of the stored type

title: Rule of zero versus manual special members
question: How do you decide whether a type should follow the rule of zero, rule of five, or use deleted operations?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the type directly managing a resource or only composing RAII members?
answerOutline: Describe when custom special members are needed
sampleAnswer: If a type only composes members that already manage themselves, I prefer the rule of zero and let the compiler generate special members because that usually gives the simplest and safest code. Once a type directly owns a raw resource such as a file descriptor, mapped region, or custom handle, I either wrap that resource in a dedicated RAII member or implement the relevant special members intentionally, for example deleting copy and making move `noexcept`. A typical pattern is `class Fd { int fd_; public: Fd(Fd&&) noexcept; Fd& operator=(Fd&&) noexcept; Fd(const Fd&) = delete; };`, which encodes unique ownership and makes container moves efficient. The mistake is writing some but not all of the operations, leaving accidental shallow copies or invariant breaks after move. The senior view is that these rules are really about invariant management: choose the smallest ownership surface, then make the type semantics obvious to both humans and the compiler.

title: Mutexes versus atomics in low-latency code
question: When do you use atomics instead of mutexes, and what mistakes do engineers make when they reach for lock-free code too early?

sampleAnswer: I start with the data ownership pattern and contention profile, not with a bias that lock-free is automatically faster. A `std::mutex` is often the right answer for infrequent or coarse-grained coordination because it is easier to reason about, while an atomic such as `std::atomic<uint64_t> seq{0};` is appropriate for tiny shared state or carefully designed SPSC handoff paths. title: Explaining acquire and release correctly
question: Explain acquire-release memory ordering and give a concrete example of when it is sufficient and when it is not.
clarifyingQuestions: Is the example single-producer/single-consumer publication or a more complex synchronization pattern?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating ability to connect theory to code
answerOutline: State what ordering it does not provide
Mention when seq_cst or fences are needed
sampleAnswer: A release store makes prior writes in that thread visible to another thread that performs a matching acquire load and observes that stored value, which is why acquire-release is the standard publication pattern. For example, a producer can write `payload`, then do `ready.store(true, std::memory_order_release);`, and the consumer can spin on `ready.load(std::memory_order_acquire)` before safely reading `payload`. That is sufficient when one atomic flag establishes visibility for the preceding non-atomic writes, but it is not a magic replacement for reasoning about all interleavings or for multi-variable protocols with no clear synchronization edge. If several independent atomics need a single total order or the reasoning is otherwise subtle, I may use stronger ordering such as `seq_cst` or redesign around a simpler handoff structure instead of scattering fences everywhere. The key senior point is to explain not just the definition, but the happens-before relationship you are deliberately creating and why it is enough for that specific state machine.
commonMistakes: Saying acquire and release are about CPU speed only
Using relaxed loads where a publication edge is required
followUps: Would acquire-release alone make a ring buffer correct?
When are fences preferable to per-operation orderings?

title: ABA and memory reclamation in lock-free structures
question: What is the ABA problem, and how would you address memory reclamation in a lock-free stack or queue?
clarifyingQuestions: Are we discussing a pointer-based structure with CAS and node reuse?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating ability to connect progress guarantees with reclamation
answerOutline: Explain why reclaimed memory makes it dangerous
Compare hazard pointers, epochs, and tagged pointers
sampleAnswer: ABA happens when a compare-exchange sees the same pointer value twice and assumes nothing changed, even though the pointed-to node may have been removed, freed, and reused in between. A classic example is `head.compare_exchange_weak(old, old->next)` on a lock-free stack: if another thread pops `old`, frees it, and allocates a new node at the same address, the CAS can succeed on a logically invalid state. Tagged pointers can reduce the ABA risk by extending identity, but they do not solve reclamation by themselves; you still need a policy such as hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation, or reference counting to ensure removed nodes are not freed while another thread may still observe them. In many low-latency systems I prefer epoch-based reclamation when thread sets are stable because it keeps the fast path simple, while hazard pointers give finer control at the cost of more per-access bookkeeping. The real senior answer is that lock-free correctness is never just about the CAS loop; reclamation strategy is part of the data structure definition.
commonMistakes: Thinking tagged pointers completely solve safe reclamation
Ignoring reclamation because tests rarely expose ABA
followUps: Would shared_ptr solve this?
What operational issues arise with stalled threads in epoch schemes?

title: Designing a bounded ring buffer correctly
question: How would you reason about correctness and performance in a bounded ring buffer shared between threads?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the queue SPSC, MPSC, or MPMC?
sampleAnswer: The first design choice is narrowing the concurrency model because an SPSC ring buffer is dramatically simpler than MPMC and often sufficient for feed or handoff stages. In an SPSC design I usually keep producer and consumer indices in separate cache lines, write the element first, then publish the updated tail with release semantics; the consumer acquires the tail before reading the element and advances its own head similarly. I want power-of-two capacity for cheap masking like `index & (capacity - 1)`, but correctness around full and empty states matters more than saving a modulus if the queue semantics are unclear. Performance issues usually come from cache-line ping-pong, unnecessary fences, or blocking behavior when the queue fills, so I define whether writers drop, spin, or backpressure the caller as part of the interface. The strong answer treats the ring buffer as a state machine with explicit publication, capacity, and shutdown contracts, not just as an array with atomics.

Putting head and tail on the same cache line
followUps: How would the design change for MPMC?

title: Condition variables and wakeup discipline
question: What are the common pitfalls with std::condition_variable, and how do you use it correctly in production code?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the wait path handling shutdown as well as normal work arrival?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating basic but important synchronization correctness
answerOutline: Discuss missed notifications and lock discipline
sampleAnswer: The first rule with `std::condition_variable` is that waits must always be predicate-based because spurious wakeups are allowed and notifications can race with the consumer's sleep transition. The standard pattern is `cv.wait(lock, [&]{ return ready || stop; });`, where the predicate is protected by the same mutex as the shared state. Common bugs are checking the condition outside the lock, using `if` instead of `while`, or forgetting to model shutdown, which leaves threads hanging forever during process exit. I also separate the condition from the work when necessary: notify after state change, keep the critical section small, and avoid assuming that `notify_one()` transfers the lock or CPU directly to the waiter. title: Explaining value categories to drive API design

title: Perfect forwarding without footguns
question: What is perfect forwarding, and what are the most common mistakes when using forwarding references?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the template forwarding into construction or into another generic call?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating template and move semantics depth

sampleAnswer: Perfect forwarding means preserving the value category of a caller's argument through a generic layer, typically using a forwarding reference `T&&` in a deduced context plus `std::forward<T>(arg)`. A classic example is `template<class T, class... Args> std::unique_ptr<T> make(Args&&... args) { return std::unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...)); }`, where lvalues stay lvalues and rvalues stay movable. title: constexpr and consteval in production code
question: When do constexpr and consteval meaningfully help in a real codebase, and when are they mostly ceremony?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the target a compile-time lookup table, protocol metadata, or validation logic?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating ability to separate useful static work from gimmicks
answerOutline: State when runtime code is better
sampleAnswer: `constexpr` is valuable when moving work to compile time improves correctness or startup cost without making the code unreadable, such as building fixed lookup tables, validating protocol constants, or precomputing masks. `consteval` is stricter and useful when something must never exist as a runtime computation, for example generating compile-time IDs or rejecting malformed configuration literals at compile time. A simple example is `constexpr auto mask = build_mask(levels);`, where the generated structure becomes part of the binary and avoids repeated runtime setup. I avoid turning ordinary business logic into metaprogramming theater, because the readability and compile-time cost can outweigh tiny startup wins, especially if the values are not actually static. The strong answer shows you know how to use compile-time computation to enforce invariants, not just to impress people with clever templates.
commonMistakes: Using constexpr where the input is not truly compile-time
Ignoring build-time cost and diagnostics complexity

When is consteval too restrictive?

title: Type traits and tag dispatch versus if constexpr
question: How do you decide between type traits, tag dispatch, specialization, and if constexpr for compile-time branching?
clarifyingQuestions: Do the branches imply different behavior, different storage, or only small implementation details?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating ability to keep generic code maintainable
answerOutline: Use if constexpr for local branching
sampleAnswer: I choose the mechanism based on how structurally different the branches are rather than on which template trick is most fashionable. If the difference is local implementation detail, `if constexpr` is usually the clearest choice because the algorithm stays in one place while dead branches are discarded at compile time. If the type needs a fundamentally different representation or optimized policy, a specialization or tag-dispatched helper can keep the main interface clean, for example selecting a fast path for trivially copyable payloads. Type traits are most useful when they capture a reusable semantic property, but I try to keep trait vocabulary small and meaningful instead of building a private meta-language nobody else understands. The senior answer is about keeping generic code readable and diagnosable while still enabling zero-cost decisions where they actually matter.

Creating many opaque custom traits with unclear semantics

title: Variadic templates and fold expressions in APIs
question: What are fold expressions good for, and what pitfalls appear when you use variadic templates in real APIs?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the variadic interface performance-driven or just trying to look flexible?
answerOutline: Discuss compile-time diagnostics and overload control
sampleAnswer: Fold expressions are a clean way to reduce parameter packs without recursive boilerplate, for example `return (... + values);` or `(sink.write(std::forward<Args>(args)), ...);`. They are great when the operation is truly associative or when I want ordered side effects in a compact generic helper, such as serializing a fixed list of fields into a buffer. The pitfalls are mostly API design issues: a variadic template can accept far more combinations than you intended, generate ugly diagnostics, and make overload sets surprising unless you constrain it carefully. I therefore pair variadics with concepts or static assertions and use them where they map to a real abstraction, not just to avoid writing three overloads. A strong answer shows that fold expressions reduce implementation noise, but the real challenge is still designing an interface whose valid argument space is understandable.
commonMistakes: Using variadics without constraints
Assuming every fold has safe ordering or associativity semantics
followUps: What happens with empty parameter packs?
How do you constrain heterogeneous variadics?

title: Benchmarking without lying to yourself
question: How do you benchmark C++ code rigorously enough to trust the result in a low-latency system?
clarifyingQuestions: Are we measuring microbenchmarks, end-to-end latency, or both?
sampleAnswer: I begin by asking what decision the benchmark is supposed to inform, because the setup for a micro-optimization test is different from the setup for end-to-end latency analysis. For microbenchmarks I pin cores, warm caches deliberately, control compiler optimization, prevent dead-code elimination, and record distributions such as p50, p99, and worst cases rather than celebrating one fast mean. I also watch for environment traps like turbo changes, allocator state, NUMA migration, and cross-talk from other processes, because nanosecond-scale claims are meaningless if the machine state is drifting underneath you. A code snippet like `benchmark([&]{ do_work(state); });` is only the starting point; I still need perf counters, traces, or replay traffic to verify the win survives realistic data shapes. The strong answer is that trustworthy benchmarking is a systems exercise, not just a loop around `std::chrono`.
commonMistakes: Reporting only average time
Running a benchmark that the optimizer can partially remove
followUps: How do you benchmark tail latency?
Would you benchmark with CPU frequency scaling enabled?

title: Data layout, cache locality, and branch behavior
question: How do data layout and branch prediction affect C++ performance, and what tradeoffs do you consider when optimizing them?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the workload streaming, random-access, or branch-heavy decision logic?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating ability to optimize layout before micro-tuning instructions
answerOutline: Discuss contiguous layout and working-set size
sampleAnswer: In many real systems, data layout dominates instruction count because a cache miss costs far more than an extra arithmetic operation, so I first try to make the working set smaller and more contiguous. That can mean preferring structure-of-arrays over array-of-structures for vectorized scans, keeping hot fields together, or splitting cold metadata out so a critical loop touches fewer cache lines. Branch prediction matters too: if one path is overwhelmingly common, shaping the code so the fast path stays linear and the rare path is deferred can reduce frontend stalls and speculation waste. I do not blindly flatten every branch or normalize every structure, because more specialized layouts can hurt maintainability or make updates expensive if the access pattern changes. The strong answer connects cache lines, branch predictability, and domain access patterns, then shows how measurement drives the final choice.
commonMistakes: Counting instructions while ignoring cache misses
Applying SOA or branchless code without checking the access pattern
followUps: When can branchless code be slower?
How would you detect false sharing versus cache miss problems?

title: Virtual dispatch in hot paths
question: What are the costs of virtual dispatch in C++, and when should you replace it with templates, variants, or other techniques?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the polymorphism on the hot path or only at system boundaries?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating ability to avoid premature devirtualization work
answerOutline: Explain indirect call and layout costs
sampleAnswer: Virtual dispatch adds an indirect branch and typically an extra pointer chase, which can matter in hot loops because it limits inlining and can hurt branch prediction and cache locality. That said, virtual interfaces are often perfectly fine at system boundaries, configuration layers, or sparse control paths where clarity and substitutability are more valuable than squeezing every cycle out of one call. If profiling shows the polymorphic call itself is on the hot path, I consider alternatives such as templates for static polymorphism, `std::variant` plus visitation for a small closed set, or a manual function table when ABI stability matters. I avoid replacing runtime polymorphism blindly, because template-based solutions can increase code size or couple too many components at compile time. A senior answer makes the tradeoff explicit: indirect calls are a cost, but the right replacement depends on ownership of types, binary shape, and measured hotspot evidence.
commonMistakes: Calling virtual dispatch always bad
Ignoring code-size blowup from template-based replacements
followUps: Can the compiler devirtualize anyway?
When is variant a poor substitute?

title: Exceptions in latency-sensitive code
question: How do you think about exceptions in a low-latency C++ codebase?
clarifyingQuestions: Are we discussing the hot trading path or broader service code around it?
interviewerIntent: Evaluating separation between hot and cold paths
answerOutline: Discuss steady-state cost versus unwind cost
Mention explicit contracts on hot paths
sampleAnswer: I separate the codebase by path: in the true latency-critical path I usually prefer explicit error channels such as status codes, `std::expected`, or prevalidated inputs so failure handling stays predictable and visible. Exceptions can still be fine in control-plane or startup code where the error is genuinely exceptional and the clarity benefit outweighs any concern about unwind cost or tooling complexity. The steady-state cost of zero-cost exceptions may be small on some platforms, but the real issue in low-latency code is that an unexpected throw can explode latency, bypass local cleanup assumptions, and complicate reasoning about invariants under stress. So my preference is not ideological avoidance; it is boundary discipline, where hot-path code has a no-throw contract and outer layers decide how errors are logged, translated, or escalated. The strong answer shows consistency: if you ban exceptions in one path, you also need interfaces, tests, and reviews that make that policy enforceable.
commonMistakes: Claiming exceptions are always free or always forbidden
Ignoring unwind behavior and invariants under failure
followUps: Would you allow exceptions during initialization?
How do you enforce no-throw on the hot path?
seniorExtension: Compare exceptions with expected-style error returns in terms of binary size, ergonomics, and policy enforcement across a large codebase.

title: Compiler optimizations, inlining, and aliasing assumptions
question: How do compiler optimization settings, inlining, and aliasing rules influence performance work in C++?
clarifyingQuestions: Is the concern whole-program optimization, hot loop generation, or portability of assumptions?
answerOutline: Discuss inlining benefits and code-size costs
sampleAnswer: A lot of C++ performance work is really about making the optimizer's job easier while not crossing into undefined behavior or unmaintainable source code. Inlining can remove call overhead and expose constant propagation, but excessive inlining can bloat the binary and hurt I-cache, so I check generated assembly or perf counters before assuming more inlining is better. Aliasing rules matter because if the compiler must assume two pointers may refer to the same memory, it will often generate more conservative loads and stores; understanding object lifetimes and strict aliasing helps explain why some transformations appear or disappear. Build settings like LTO and PGO can be extremely powerful because they broaden visibility and hot-path knowledge, but they also change debugging and build complexity, so I use them as part of a measurement-driven pipeline rather than as a magic switch. The strong answer is that source changes, compiler flags, and generated code all need to line up before you can claim a real optimization.
commonMistakes: Assuming force-inline always improves speed
Relying on undefined behavior to coerce better code generation
followUps: What is strict aliasing?
How would you use PGO in a replay-based trading workload?
